XII. Standing against the Strategies of the Devil (6:10–20)

A. Wearing God’s Protective Armor (6:10–17)

B. Persevering in Watchful Prayer (6:18–20)


B. Persevering in Watchful Prayer (6:18–20)

In order to stand against the strategies of the devil and other evil powers, believers must, in addition to putting on the armor of God, pray with constancy, devotion, and alertness. This new section is tied grammatically to 6:10–20 by the dependence of the two participles in 6:18 on the imperative δέξασθε (dexasthe, receive) in 6:17. Thematically, however, the section begins a new train of thought. The military imagery largely disappears, and Paul now focuses on a straightforward appeal to his readers to devote themselves to prayer for all believers, and especially for him.

The section can be divided into two main parts. First, in 6:18a Paul formulates a highly repetitive, and therefore emphatic, exhortation to his readers to devote themselves to prayer. Second, in 6:18b–20 he describes the object of their prayers. This second main part briefly urges his readers to pray for all God’s people and then asks them, in much more detail, to pray for him in light of the tension he is experiencing between his status as a prisoner and his calling to proclaim the mystery of the gospel.



Exegesis and Exposition

18. . . praying at all times in the Spirit, through every prayer and urgent petition, and being watchful in this very thing with all devotion and urgent petition for all the saints, 19and for me, that speech might be given me when I open my mouth to make known with boldness the mystery ⌜of the gospel⌝ 20(for which I serve as an enchained ambassador) that, ⌜with respect to it⌝, I might speak boldly, as I must.

[6:18] Paul now moves away from the image of the armor of God and exhorts his readers to engage in prayer. The main verbal elements in 6:18–20 are the two participles here in 6:18, προσευχόμενοι (proseuchomenoi, praying) and ἀγρυπνοῦντες (agrypnountes, being watchful). It is difficult to know exactly how these participles are related to the rest of the section. Some interpreters put a period at the end of 6:17, indicating that the two participles are part of a new sentence. If this is correct, then they must be understood imperatively (“pray . . . watch”), and there is precedent for this in Rom. 12:9–21 (Sellin 2008: 484n79).

In Robertson’s judgment, however, “no participle should be explained in this way that can properly be connected with a finite verb” (1923: 1134; quoted in Wallace 1996: 650). Two finite verbs could supply the needed connection: στῆτε (stēte, stand) in 6:14 and δέξασθε (dexasthe, receive) in 6:17. If the participles go with στῆτε, then they join the list of pieces of armor to indicate a seventh means by which believers can stand their ground against the devil’s onslaught: they can stand by paying careful attention to prayer. Στῆτε, however, is too far from these two participles to function plausibly as the main verb to which they are related. This leaves δέξασθε, and attaching the participles to this imperative is a more reasonable way to understand the syntax (Fee 1994: 730; Hoehner 2002: 854).

Still, this explanation is not entirely satisfactory. Paul does not develop the thought that his readers should receive salvation and the word of God by praying and watching, which is, strictly speaking, the meaning the syntax would demand. Instead, a simple and straightforward focus on the need for prayer replaces the military imagery.

The two participles, then, are probably used loosely in a way similar to the use of ὑποτασσόμενοι (hypotassomenoi, submitting) in 5:21. There too the participle is syntactically related to the imperative πληροῦσθε (plērousthe) in 5:18, but the thought has shifted away from the results of being filled in the Spirit (speaking, singing, making melody, giving thanks) to the imperatival thought that believers should submit to one another. The participles in both 5:21 and here are being used adverbially and are related to the imperative-mood verb that occurs before them, but these participles adopt an independent, imperatival quality of their own.

The result of all this for interpreting the passage is that Paul somewhat enigmatically begins a new thought with two participles formally related to a main verb they do not really explain. Instead, his participles introduce a new subject. He was probably still thinking of ways in which his readers could hold their ground in the struggle against the devil and his powerful spiritual allies, but he has dropped the military imagery and decided to devote a lengthy “sentence” to prayer.

His readers’ prayers should have five characteristics. First, he urges them to pray constantly. The initial phrase διὰ πάσης προσευχῆς καὶ δεήσεως (dia pasēs proseuchēs kai deēseōs, through every prayer and urgent petition), with its redundancy and its stress on the variety of prayer, communicates the need for frequent prayer. The phrase ἐν παντὶ καιρῷ (en panti kairō) meaning “at all times” (cf. Ps. 33:2 LXX [34:2 MT; 34:1 Eng.]; Tob. 4:19 Vat.; 14:98 Sin.; Luke 21:36), performs the same function but more explicitly. Prayers should not be reserved only for certain occasions but should be a constant activity of the believer (cf. 1 Thess. 5:17) and therefore as varied in their subject matter as the circumstances of life itself.

Second, Paul’s readers should pray “in the Spirit” (ἐν πνεύματι, en pneumati). When Paul connects prayer with the Spirit elsewhere, he seems to refer to prayer that the Spirit empowers (Rom. 8:26; cf. Fee 1994: 731). This is not merely prayer “in the sphere of the Spirit,” as many commentators have thought (e.g., Eadie 1883: 475; Heil 2007a: 290), or “spirited” or heartfelt prayer (e.g., Westcott 1906: 97), but prayer that the Spirit has given the believer the strength to utter.[1]

Third, they should be alert and attentive to constant prayer. The phrase εἰς αὐτό (eis auto) means “for this [or that] purpose” (cf. Josephus, Ant. 12.15; 19.208) and refers back to the constant prayer in the previous clause. If Paul’s readers are to pray as much as they need to, then they will have to be attentive to the task. The verb ἀγρυπνέω (agrypneō) means basically “lie awake, pass sleepless nights” (LSJ 16) and was used in eschatological contexts in early Christianity of the need for believers to “stay awake” as they awaited the coming of the Son of Man (Mark 13:33). This means being busy about the work the Master has assigned them (13:34). It means not lapsing into debauched and drunken behavior, but instead being watchful (ἀγρυπνεῖτε) in prayer in order to escape the coming judgment (Luke 21:34–36). Paul is also concerned that the readers of Ephesians avoid “the unfruitful works of darkness” (5:11) and the “wrath of God” that will come to those who are involved in such works (5:6). Perhaps this request that they be watchful in prayer arises in part out of that concern (cf. 1 Thess. 5:4–11; Rom. 13:11–14). Being attentive to prayer is one way of walking carefully and wisely, of “redeeming the time,” in light of the evil days in which they live (5:15).

Fourth, they should be zealous in their devotion to prayer. The noun προσκαρτέρησις (proskarterēsis) is a rare word, appearing prior to Ephesians only twice: once in a second-century-BC inscription from the island of Andros and once in the first-century-BC philosopher Philodemus. Philodemus’s use of the term to speak of recounting arguments in “painstaking detail” is not particularly illuminating.[2] The Andros inscription, however, is more helpful. It refers to an admired physician who “gave himself over” (ἐπέδωκεν ἑαυτόν, epedōken heauton) to his profession with “particular devotion” (προσκαρτέρησις).[3] Here too Paul urges believers to give themselves over to prayer with the kind of enthusiasm and zeal normally associated with the committed practice of a craft or trade (cf. Col. 4:2; Acts 1:14; 2:42, 46; 6:4).

Fifth, they should pray for all God’s people (περὶ πάντων τῶν ἁγίων, peri pantōn tōn hagiōn). Their “urgent petition” (δέησις, deēsis) should not merely focus on themselves and their own battle with the evil one and his forces, but should also include all other believers and the battle against the devil that all face together.

To summarize, Paul urges his readers to defend their position in Christ against the onslaught of evil by prayer that is constant, Spirit-empowered, alert to surrounding evil, zealous in its devotion, and ecumenical in its breadth.

[6:19–20] Next, Paul asks his readers to pray for him personally because, in light of his legal troubles, he needs courage to proclaim with clarity and freedom the mystery contained in the gospel.

Paul frequently asked the congregations who read his letters to pray for him and his coworkers (1 Thess. 5:25; 2 Thess. 3:1; 2 Cor. 1:11; Rom. 15:30–32; Col. 4:3–4), and he asked for prayer specifically for himself when the success of his witness to the gospel was under threat from outside circumstances (Rom. 15:30–32; Col. 4:3b–4; cf. Phil. 1:19; Philem. 22). The problem here is that Paul is wearing a “chain” (ἅλυσις, halysis) because he is a prisoner. Presumably the situation in which he will have an opportunity to explain the gospel is a legal hearing of some kind. Since his proclamation of the gospel to the Gentiles was the cause of his imprisonment (3:1), and since he would present his defense before a Roman magistrate, it is understandable that he would be tempted either not to explain the gospel at all, or in explaining it to leave out critical elements that might be politically sensitive.

Paul knows that he must not yield to this temptation because, despite his imprisonment, he “serves as an ambassador” (πρεσβεύω, presbeuō; 2 Cor. 5:20). Someone who served as an ambassador in the eastern Roman Empire was charged with traveling to a specific destination for the purpose of communicating the interests of another party to those in power in that other place (Bash 1997: 4). Paul’s use of the term here fits with the picture he has developed of himself in 3:1–13 as responsible for administering the gift that God has given him to preach to the Gentiles the mystery of their inclusion in the people of God (3:2–3, 6), a responsibility that, despite its importance, has landed him in prison (3:1, 13).

Here in 6:19 Paul emphasizes that if he is to be faithful to his ambassadorial role, he must explain the mystery of the gospel with clarity and candor. So he asks for prayer by using a series of expressions referring to speech that is both divinely inspired and straightforward. The Scriptures sometimes describe God as opening the mouth of his spokesperson (e.g., Exod. 4:12 LXX; 4:15; Num. 22:28; Ezek. 3:27; 29:21 LXX; 33:22; cf. Prov. 31:8 LXX; Luke 1:64), and Paul can use that expression elsewhere to refer to candid speech (2 Cor. 6:11). Both the noun παρρησία (parrēsia) and the verb παρρησιάζομαι (parrēsiazomai), moreover, were used to describe boldness in speaking the truth freely, especially in the presence of powerful people (e.g., Let. Aris. 125; Acts 4:13, 29; Josephus, Ant. 16.377–78). Paul has already used παρρησία with this meaning of the straightforward communication believers have with God because they are “in Christ” (3:12).[4] Paul has reminded the Thessalonians that when he was among them, he preached the gospel with this sort of clarity and boldness, despite the suffering he was experiencing (1 Thess. 2:2; cf. 2 Cor. 3:12; Phil. 1:20), and early Christian tradition remembers Paul’s bold proclamation of the gospel as a characteristic of his ministry (Acts 9:27–28; 14:3; 19:8; 26:26; 28:31).

Paul describes the message that he wants to give as τὸ μυστήριον τοῦ εὐαγγελίου (to mystērion tou euangeliou, the mystery of the gospel). This refers to the mystery defined earlier in the letter and contained in the gospel. It is the revelation that Jews and Gentiles are being brought together as they believe the gospel and become part of Christ’s body (3:3–6, 9–10). It is also the revelation that this social unity is part of a cosmic unity that will eventually embrace everything in the heavens and on earth (1:9–10), including “all rule and authority and power and lordship” (1:21). This may have been precisely the element of the mystery that Paul was tempted to leave out of any testimony before a government official.[5]

Summary

In 6:18–20 Paul urges his readers to pray as part of their defense against evil. Their prayer activity should be more than an avocation or a sideline. It should be characterized by enormous breadth—they should pray at all times and for all the saints—and should be energized both by their own zeal and by the Spirit’s power.

Paul considers himself to be one of the saints for whom they should pray. He is an ambassador of the gospel mystery, that God is uniting all people groups by means of his enthroned, anointed king and has placed all other powers and authorities under Jesus’s feet. Yet he is also in chains and knows full well that this message will be difficult to deliver faithfully to those who have imprisoned him. He asks his readers, then, for prayer that he might have courage to explain the gospel—even this politically sensitive element of it—with clarity and courage when the opportunity arises for him to speak.



Additional Notes

6:19. The phrase τοῦ εὐαγγελίου does not appear in the important Alexandrian manuscript B (Vat.) and in significant witnesses from the Western tradition (F, G, some manuscripts of the Old Latin, Victorinus of Rome, and Ambrosiaster). The presence of the phrase, however, has strong testimony from the Alexandrian (א, A, I, Ψ, 33, 1739), Western (D), and Byzantine traditions (most manuscripts). Although the phrase might have been added in an attempt to make the reference to τὸ μυστήριον more specific, τοῦ εὐαγγελίου would be an odd way to do this, since τοῦ Χριστοῦ and τοῦ θεοῦ were more readily available in 3:4; Col. 2:2; and 4:3 (Metzger 1994: 542). This consideration, combined with the strong manuscript support for the longer reading, make it probable that Paul wrote τὸ μυστήριον τοῦ εὐαγγελίου.

6:20. Several witnesses either place ἐν αὐτῷ after παρρησιάσωμαι (e.g., א, 104, 459) or, instead of ἐν αὐτῷ, have the simple accusative pronoun αὐτό (𝔓46, B, 1739, 1881). The coalescence of 𝔓46, א, B, and 1739 (all from the Alexandrian tradition) around a reading other than ἐν αὐτῷ παρρησιάσωαμι is impressive, but neither alternative to the more widely accepted reading is likely to be what Paul wrote. The reading with αὐτό is both reminiscent of Col. 4:4 (Best 1998: 609) and stylistically more concise (Metzger 1994: 542), and the reading with ἐν αὐτῷ following παρρησιάσωμαι probably preserves a less unexpected word order (cf. Col. 4:4; Ps. 11:6 LXX [12:6 MT; 12:5 Eng.], quoted in 1 Clem. 15.7; Acts 9:27–28). The witnesses for ἐν αὐτῷ παρρησιάσωμαι, moreover, form an impressive array from a broad spread of traditions—e.g., A, I, Ψ, 6, 33, 81 (Alexandrian); D, F, G (Western); and most Byzantine manuscripts. This reading, then, is likely to be correct. In any case, the meaning “with respect to it, I might speak boldly” remains unaffected.





X. Avoiding and Transforming the Deeds of Darkness (5:3–14)

XI. Wise Conduct within the Household (5:15–6:9)

XII. Standing against the Strategies of the Devil (6:10–20)

XIII. A Concluding Commendation and a Final Prayer-Wish (6:21–24)


XIII. A Concluding Commendation and a Final Prayer-Wish (6:21–24)

Paul signals the final major division of the letter with the conjunction δέ (de, now; cf. 3:20; 5:3). The purpose of this concluding section is first to describe the mission and character of Tychicus, the letter’s courier, and second to provide the letter with a fitting conclusion in the form of two brief prayers for all believers, one that they might experience peace, love, and faith, and the other that they might experience grace. The section, then, falls neatly into two paragraphs, and in its broad structure it follows a pattern familiar from other letters in the Pauline corpus.

Near the conclusion of many of his letters, Paul requests prayer for himself, speaks of his (or his coworkers’) travel plans, and utters a prayer-wish that his readers would experience God’s peace. All his letters end with a prayer-wish for God’s grace. These standard elements also appear in Ephesians. He requests prayer for himself, a request that we have examined in the previous section since it flowed naturally out of the admonition he gave his readers to be diligent in prayer for their fellow believers (6:18–19; cf. 1 Thess. 5:25; Rom. 15:30–33; Col. 4:18b). He discusses the travel plans of Tychicus, who, it is implied, is the letter’s courier and who will both tell the letter’s readers about Paul’s circumstances and provide encouragement for them (6:21–22; cf. 1 Cor. 16:5–12; Phil. 4:15–20; 2 Cor. 13:1–10; Rom. 15:14–29; Philem. 22; Col. 4:7–9; Titus 3:12–13; 2 Tim. 4:9–13). He also concludes the letter with a double prayer-wish that peace and grace might come to his readers (6:23–24; cf. 1 Thess. 5:23, 28; 2 Thess. 3:16, 18; Gal. 6:16, 18; Phil. 4:9, 23; 2 Cor. 13:11, 13; Rom. 15:13, 33; 16:20).

Various elements show up in other Pauline letters that are not present here: practical instruction about church leadership (1 Thess. 5:12–13; Gal. 6:6; 1 Cor. 16:15–18); brief, pithy ethical instruction (1 Thess. 5:13–22; Gal. 6:7–10; 1 Cor. 16:13–14; 2 Cor. 13:11; Rom. 16:17–19; Col. 4:17; Titus 3:14); a command to have the letter read to the whole group (1 Thess. 5:27; Col. 4:16); or a Pauline autograph (2 Thess. 3:17; Gal. 6:11), sometimes in the form of a greeting (1 Cor. 16:21; Col. 4:18). But none of these elements appears invariably, and so it is not particularly surprising that they are absent from Ephesians.[1]

Ephesians does have two unique characteristics, however, that are more surprising in a Pauline letter. First, both the prayer-wish for peace and the prayer-wish for grace are in the third person (“Peace to the brothers [and sisters]. . . . Grace be with all those who love our Lord Jesus Christ”), whereas elsewhere in the Pauline corpus the peace wish, where it occurs, is normally in the second person (Gal. 6:16 is the exception), and the grace-wish is always in the second person. This unusual element is probably yet another sign that the letter was intended for all the Christians in the various house churches in Ephesus, many of whom Paul did not know personally after his nearly seven-year absence from the city.

Second, most of 6:21 and all of 6:22 duplicate, word for word, Col. 4:7–8. Apart from the two words καὶ σύνδουλος (kai syndoulos, and fellow slave) in Col. 4:7, the agreement in wording between the two passages involves “twenty-nine consecutive words” (Mitton 1951: 59). The most reasonable explanation for this oddity is that the author of one letter—or his secretary—had before him, and copied out, the words of the other letter (Lincoln 1990: lv; cf. Mitton 1951: 59; Sellin 2008: 490). Although this is unique in a Pauline letter, it is not unprecedented among ancient letters generally. Ignatius also included an identical commendation of the letter courier Burrhus in two different letters, composed at the same time and sent to separate destinations (Ign. Phld. 11.2; Ign. Smyrn. 12.1).[2] This unusual feature of Ephesians is probably a result of the specific circumstances under which it was composed: Paul sent Ephesians, Colossians, and Philemon with Tychicus, and after composing the description of Tychicus’s mission and his commendation for Colossians, instructed his secretary to repeat them in Ephesians. This was done with a few, probably unconscious, changes.[3]

In sum, Paul ends Ephesians in a way that is broadly similar to the conclusions of his other letters, but with some unique features prompted by the historical situation out of which Ephesians arose. He tells his readers about the mission and character of Tychicus and then turns again to prayer, asking that all faithful believers experience “peace,” “love,” “grace,” and “faith.”





XIII. A Concluding Commendation and a Final Prayer-Wish (6:21–24)

A. Tychicus and His Mission (6:21–22)

B. Peace, Love, Faith, and Grace for the Letter’s Recipients (6:23–24)


A. Tychicus and His Mission (6:21–22)

In the first subsection of the letter’s conclusion, Paul both describes Tychicus’s mission and commends him to the recipients as a reliable messenger. Tychicus will fill in the details about Paul’s circumstances that the written letter does not provide, and he will encourage the hearts of Paul’s readers, who according to 3:13 were discouraged precisely because of the suffering that Paul was experiencing. We do not know what form this encouragement took, but perhaps it looked something like what Paul says of his suffering in Phil. 1:12–18b. There he describes his difficult circumstances (τὰ κατ᾿ ἐμέ, ta kat’ eme, my circumstances; cf. Eph. 6:21) as problems that do not really matter because through them “Christ is being preached, and in this I rejoice” (Phil. 1:18b).

Paul also wants his readers to know that Tychicus is a reliable messenger. He is, Paul says, not only a fellow believer but also a dear friend and a trustworthy assistant in the work that the Lord has given Paul and his coworkers to do.



Exegesis and Exposition

21Now, that ⌜you too⌝ might know my circumstances—how I am doing—Tychicus, the beloved brother and faithful servant in the Lord, will make everything known to you, 22whom I have sent to you for this very thing, that you might know our circumstances and that he may encourage your hearts.

[6:21–22] Paul begins and ends his description of Tychicus with a reference to Tychicus’s mission (6:21a, 22b). Tychicus will let the readers of Ephesians know all about Paul’s circumstances.[1] The redundancy of Paul’s Greek is remarkable, even in a letter as redundant as Ephesians. He uses three phrases to refer to his circumstances, τὰ κατ᾿ ἐμε (ta kat’ eme, my circumstances), τί πράσσω (ti prassō, how I am doing), and τὰ περὶ ἡμῶν (ta peri hēmōn, our circumstances). The plural in the third phrase probably refers to Paul and Tychicus (Best 1998: 616),[2] and the redundancy probably emphasizes how full Tychicus’s account of his and Paul’s circumstances will be. He “will make everything [πάντα, panta] known to you,” Paul assures them. He similarly uses two phrases to show that it is precisely to make known his and Tychicus’s circumstances that Tychicus is coming, ἵνα . . . εἰδῆτε καὶ ὑμεῖς (hina . . . eidēte kai hymeis, that you too might know) and εἰς αὐτὸ τοῦτο, ἵνα γνῶτε (eis auto touto, hina gnōte, for this very thing, that you might know). It is difficult to escape the impression that the oral account Tychicus would give of what Paul has been experiencing will be a vital supplement to what the apostle has written in the letter.[3]

Paul commends Tychicus to his readers with two phrases. He is first a “beloved brother” (ἀγαπητὸς ἀδελφός, agapētos adelphos), a phrase that Paul also applies to Onesimus in Philem. 16 (cf. Col. 4:9). The use of sibling language for fellow believers is characteristic of the Pauline corpus, and Paul frequently refers to others by name as “beloved” (1 Cor. 4:17; Rom. 16:5, 8, 9, 12; Col. 1:7; 4:7, 9, 14; Philem. 1; 2 Tim. 1:2; Acts 15:25). The phrase probably means that the person is especially close to Paul; he can use it of Onesimus, who is his “very heart” (Philem. 16), and of Timothy, whom he considers to be his “beloved and faithful child” (1 Cor. 4:17).

Second, Paul describes Tychicus as “a faithful servant [διάκονος, diakonos] in the Lord.” In Paul’s time the term διάκονος could already refer to someone with important responsibilities in the church (Phil. 1:1; 1 Tim. 3:8, 12; 4:6), but it continued to carry connotations of menial service, such as a “courier” or “assistant” might perform (BDAG 230–31). It carries this second sense here; Tychicus has proved himself to be a reliable coworker in the practical details of spreading the gospel. This picture is consistent with what we know of him from the three other NT references to him. He was trustworthy enough to be selected as a representative from Asia to accompany Paul’s collection for the needy believers in Jerusalem (Acts 20:4; cf. Acts 24:17; 1 Cor. 16:1–4).[4] He apparently not only carried Ephesians to its destination, but also took Paul’s letters to the Colossians and to Philemon along to Colossae (Col. 4:7–9).[5] Later Paul would contemplate sending him to Crete to take over the work of Titus among the young churches on that island (Titus 3:12), and eventually Paul sent him to Ephesus again (2 Tim. 4:12).

In a culture where the only postal service was for the exclusive use of government officials, letters often had to travel with relatively unknown people who happened to be going in the right direction (Richards 2004: 177–82; Head 2009: 284). Sometimes finding a reliable courier posed a problem. “I have been slow about sending one [a letter], for lack of a safe messenger,” Cicero wrote to Atticus in the first century BC. “There are very few who can carry a letter of weight without lightening it by perusal” (Att. 1.13; quoted in Richards 2004: 181; cf. Head 2009: 283–84). Paul wants those who read this letter to know that the contents are safe with Tychicus (cf. Phil. 2:25–30; Rom. 16:1–2).

Summary

As Paul draws his letter to a close, he commends its courier, Tychicus, as his good friend and fellow believer, and a faithful worker in the Lord’s service. He has trusted Tychicus to take the letter to its readers safely and to convey accurately the important information about Paul’s circumstances that supplements the letter’s contents.



Additional Note

6:21. Commentators have argued at length about the meaning of the καί in the phrase καὶ ὑμεῖς. If Tychicus will “also” let the readers of Ephesians know Paul’s circumstances, then who else did Paul have in mind? Some commentators have thought that Paul had himself in mind—he had discussed his readers’ circumstances in detail, and now it was their turn to find out about him (Alford 1857: 144; cf. Schnackenburg 1991: 288). Others believe that καί refers to the churches on Tychicus’s itinerary (Robinson 1904: 217), especially the church in Colossae (Haupt 1902a: 245; Hoehner 2002: 869). Still others think there was no one else in mind at all: “Paul” was using καί imprecisely, perhaps to emphasize the following ὑμεῖς (Lincoln 1990: 464–65; Best 1998: 614–15).

It is true that καί is sometimes used imprecisely in Ephesians (1:15; 2:1; Best 1998: 615), but this is not usual, and it seems better to opt for an explanation that gives the word its normal significance if at all possible. Unless one is convinced on other grounds that Ephesians is pseudonymous, the most plausible explanation seems to be that Paul was sending Tychicus not only with Ephesians, but also with Colossians and Philemon as well. If so, then he assumed that the readers of Ephesians would know that Tychicus had also been charged with telling the Colossians about Paul’s circumstances. Sellin (2008) is so convinced that καί must be given this significance that he opts for it, although he thinks the letter is pseudonymous. The verisimilitude created, he argues, is actually part of the pseudonymous author’s strategy to convince his readers the letter is authentically Paul’s (Sellin 2008: 490–91). It is equally plausible, however, to take the air of reality created by this small detail as evidence that both Ephesians and Colossians are genuine epistles of Paul, composed at about the same time and dispatched with Tychicus to their different destinations.





XIII. A Concluding Commendation and a Final Prayer-Wish (6:21–24)

A. Tychicus and His Mission (6:21–22)

B. Peace, Love, Faith, and Grace for the Letter’s Recipients (6:23–24)


B. Peace, Love, Faith, and Grace for the Letter’s Recipients (6:23–24)

Paul concludes the letter with a double prayer-wish that succinctly reminds his readers of four important themes within the letter. He prays that all believers (not simply the letter’s readers) might experience both peace and love, and he connects love with faith. He then offers a separate prayer-wish that those who love the Lord Jesus Christ “incorruptibly” might experience God’s grace.

In this quartet of abstract qualities, it is true that faith takes a subordinate role syntactically. Paul prays primarily for peace, love, and grace. In a letter that connects God’s love for his people and the love of God’s people for one another so clearly with faith (1:15; 3:17), however, it would be a mistake to make too much of this syntactical subordination.

Faith redefines existence, placing it “in Christ,” where the blessings of peace (both peace with God and peace with others) and love (both God’s love for his people and their love for one another) are freely given to God’s people as demonstrations of his grace. Much of the letter has been about this peace, love, and grace that the letter’s readers, like all God’s people, have appropriated by faith in the gospel of the Lord Jesus Christ.



Exegesis and Exposition

23Peace to the brothers [and sisters], and love with faith, from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. 24Grace be with all those who love our Lord Jesus Christ incorruptibly. ⌜ ⌝

[6:23] Paul often concludes his letters with a prayer-wish for God’s peace (εἰρήνη, eirēnē) to rest on his readers (1 Thess. 5:23; 2 Thess. 3:16; Gal. 6:16; cf. Rom. 15:33; cf. Phil. 4:9; 2 Cor. 13:11; Rom. 16:20). In Ephesians, however, peace is such an important theme that Paul probably intended his readers to recall how he had defined it specifically in the preceding letter (Gnilka 1971: 324; Lincoln 1990: 466). Christ, he had said, is “peace” for believers because through his death on the cross he had set aside the Mosaic law and so made peace between Gentiles and Jews, and between humanity generally and God (2:14–18). Later he urges his readers to maintain the social unity that God’s Spirit has brought to believers, and to do this by using “peace” as a “fastener” to hold the church together (4:3). As we have just seen in the discussion of the armor of God, “peace” is such an important element of the gospel that Paul can call it “the gospel of peace,” and he urges his readers to be ready for battle against the divisive spiritual forces of the cosmos by equipping themselves with the gospel defined in precisely these terms (6:15). According to this concluding prayer-wish, this is the peace that Paul wants God to give his readers.

In every letter but this one, Paul’s concluding prayer-wishes are formulated in the second person (e.g., “And may the peace of God himself sanctify you [ὑμᾶς, hymas] completely”; 1 Thess. 5:23). Here Paul prays, less intimately, for peace to rest on “the brothers [and sisters]” (οἱ ἀδελφοί, ho adelphoi). The term ἀδελφοί (adelphoi) was commonly used among Jews in antiquity to refer to fellow Jews (e.g., Deut. 18:15; Ps. 22:22 Eng. [22:23 MT; 21:23 LXX]; Rom. 9:3), and the early Jewish-Christian community continued this practice (Matt. 5:22, 47; 7:3; 18:15; Acts 3:22; 7:37; Heb. 2:12). Jesus seems to have given this sort of figurative family language new meaning by defining it in terms of those who do God’s will by sitting specifically under his teaching. Those who do this, he says, are “my brother and sister and mother” (Mark 3:33–35; cf. Matt. 12:48–50; Luke 8:21; 2 Clem. 9.11–10.1).

Whether Paul has derived this language from Judaism, from Jesus, from its common use in other Greco-Roman religious contexts, in Hellenistic letters, or from some combination of these is unknown, but he uses the term ἀδελφός figuratively more often than any other NT author (130 times), and like Jesus, he could expand the figure.[1] He sometimes refers to himself as the “mother” or “father” of those whom he has persuaded to believe the gospel (1 Thess. 2:7, 11; Gal. 4:19; 1 Cor. 4:15; Philem. 10; cf. 1 Cor. 4:17; Phil. 2:22), to Jesus as the “brother” of believers (Rom. 8:29), and to all believers as “brothers [and sisters]” of one another.[2] The heavy concentration of familial language in the Pauline Letters may result from the alienation that Pauline Christians felt from their families and societies after their conversion (cf. Malherbe 2000: 110).

Paul also prays that the brothers and sisters who read this letter will experience “love with faith” (ἀγάπη μετὰ πίστεως, agapē meta pisteōs). Like peace, love has been an important theme throughout the letter, whether the love of believers for one another (1:4, 15; 4:15, 16; 5:2) or the love of God (or Christ) for believers (2:4; 3:17; 5:2). Faith, too, has been an important theme. Paul’s readers were saved from rebellion against God and given a new existence “in Christ” when they put their faith in the gospel (1:13, 15; 2:8–10; 3:12). This close relationship was rooted and grounded in the love of God (and Christ) for them (3:17; 5:2), and its sacrificial nature forms a pattern that they should imitate in their love for one another (5:2, 25). Thus when Paul in 6:23 prays for his readers to experience “love with faith,” he expresses the hope that their knowledge of God’s love for them, and the love for each other that flows from this knowledge, might flourish in the fertile soil of their faith in the gospel.

All of this—peace, love, and the faith that accompanies love—comes “from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.” Although elements of the peace and love for which Paul has prayed, and all of the faith that accompanies love, are attitudes and actions of human beings, those who have and do these virtues cannot take credit for them. If God answers Paul’s prayer-wish, then these qualities will be gifts of God, just like the grace and peace that Paul has wished for his readers at the beginning of the letter (1:2).

[6:24] Like every other letter in the Pauline corpus, the concluding lines of Ephesians contain a prayer-wish for God’s grace. Elsewhere these prayer-wishes are formulated in the second-person plural and are relatively simple requests, with slight variations, that the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ might be with the letter’s readers (1 Thess. 5:28; 2 Thess. 3:18; Gal. 6:18; 1 Cor. 16:23; Phil. 4:23; 2 Cor. 13:13 [13:14 KJV]; Rom. 16:20; Philem. 25), or in most of the later Pauline letters, simply that grace might be with them (Col. 4:18; Eph. 6:24; 1 Tim. 6:21; Titus 3:15; 2 Tim. 4:22).[3]

Only 2 Cor. 13:13 and Eph. 6:24 show wide variations in the pattern, and they vary it in completely different ways. In 2 Cor. 13:13 Paul departs from the pattern with a threefold reference to grace, love, and fellowship, and an identification of the origin of each of these three gifts with a person of the Trinity. Here in Eph. 6:24 Paul seems to shift the frequent reference to the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ into the reference to the recipients of this grace, and his description of the recipients becomes the most elaborate of these descriptions in the Pauline corpus. They are “all those who love our Lord Jesus Christ incorruptibly.”

As interpreters have often noticed, this is the positive counterpart to 1 Cor. 16:22: “If anyone does not love [φιλεῖ, philei] the Lord, let him be accursed.” Moreover, the notion that God’s people are obligated to love God is prominent in both Old and New Testaments (e.g., Exod. 20:6; Deut. 5:10; 6:5; Judg. 5:31; Neh. 1:5; Ps. 145:20 MT, Eng. [144:20 LXX]; Rom. 8:28; 1 Cor. 2:9; 8:3; James 1:12; 2:5) and in other Jewish literature of the period (Sir. 1:10; 2:15–16; 34:16, 19; Pss. Sol 4.25; 6.6; 10.3; 14.1; T. Iss. 7.6; T. Dan 5.3; T. Jos. 11.1; T. Benj. 3.1; cf. Hoehner 2002: 874–75; Aletti 2001: 319n19). Although this is an unusual statement for a concluding Pauline grace-wish, then, there is precedent for a reference to the importance of loving the Lord Jesus at the end of a Pauline letter, and nothing surprising from the perspective of early Christian theology about defining the people of God in terms of those who love the Lord Jesus.

The concluding prepositional phrase ἐν ἀφθαρσίᾳ (en aphtharsia) does come as a surprise, however, and has left interpreters puzzled (Sellin 2008: 494). The term ἀφθαρσία means “incorruptibility, immortality” (BDAG 155; cf. Robinson 1904: 217–18) and had a long history of use in Greek philosophical discussion over the eternity of God, the human soul, and the world.[4] Hellenistic Jewish texts also used the term to refer to human beings who, because they were made in God’s image, were immortal (Wis. 2:23; cf. 6:19; cf. Philo, Flight 59), to martyrs whose physical frame might be torn apart but whose immortality could not be damaged by their tormentors (4 Macc. 9:22; 17:12), and to the incorruptible, eternal existence of those who love wisdom (Wis. 6:18; cf. Rom. 2:7; Philo, Agriculture 100; Drunkenness 140). The term often stands in contrast to mortal, changeable, and corruptible existence (e.g., 1 Cor. 15:42, 50, 53, 54; 2 Tim. 1:10; Philo, Creation 153; Drunkenness 140; Heir 35; Abraham 55; Moses 2.194).

If this is the meaning of the term, however, it is difficult to understand precisely what ἐν ἀφθαρσίᾳ would signify in this context. From the perspective of the sentence’s syntax, the most obvious way to take the phrase is as a modifier of τῶν ἀγαπώντων (tōn agapōntōn, those who love). But what could it mean to speak of people who love the Lord Jesus “in immortality”?

Some interpreters have taken the expression to refer to an unceasing (Hoehner 2002: 877) or persistent (Best 1998: 620) love. Neither of these options, however, are obvious translations for the term ἀφθαρσία, whose connotations of ceaselessness and eternality are derived only from the notion that what is ἄφθαρτος (aphthartos, imperishable) is not subject to decomposition.

Others believe that the phrase is not connected specifically with any element in the preceding sentence but serves rather as a rhetorical flourish loosely affiliated with the whole sentence and, to some extent, the whole letter. Believers, argues Heil (2007a: 306), are those who have been made alive, raised, and seated with Christ (2:5–6). They therefore exist in the realm of “immortality,” and it is in this realm that the truths the letter has expressed find their reality (cf. Barth 1974: 814; Sellin 2008: 494). This explanation preserves the normal meaning of ἀφθαρσία but has the disadvantage of sacrificing the most obvious way of taking the syntax.

Many other interpreters connect the phrase with the initial word χάρις (charis, grace) and take the preposition ἐν (en, in) as a conjunction that joins “the following word to one or more preceding words so as to complete a series” (Bruce 1984: 416).[5] This solution has the merit of giving ἀφθαρσία its most obvious meaning at the same time that it renders the sentence perfectly intelligible. Paul’s prayer-wish would be that “those who love our Lord Jesus Christ” be blessed with both “grace and immortality,” and this fits nicely with the letter’s emphasis on the eternal character of God’s grace toward his people (2:7; Lincoln 1990: 468). The phrase ἐν ἀφθαρσίᾳ, however, is too far from χάρις to make this understanding of the sentence plausible.

The solution to the puzzle of this closing phrase may lie in comparing the structure and meaning of the entire sentence to an ascription of praise that concludes Pss. Sol. 6.﻿[6] This brief psalm describes the blessings that come to the person whose inner character is disposed to call spontaneously on the Lord in prayer at the beginning and end of the day and throughout the vicissitudes of life. It concludes in much the same way that Paul concludes Ephesians:

Psalms of Solomon 6.6 Ephesians 6:24

εὐλογητὸς κύριος ὁ ποιῶν

eulogētos kyrios ho poiōn

Blessed be the Lord who does

ἔλεος

eleos

mercy ἡ χάρις

hē charis

Grace be

τοῖς ἀγαπῶσιν

tois agapōsin

to those who love μετὰ πάντων τῶν ἀγαπώντων

meta pantōn tōn agapōntōn

with all those who love

αὐτὸν

auton

him τὸν κύριον ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν

ton kyrion hēmōn Iēsoun Christon

our Lord Jesus Christ

ἐν ἀληθείᾳ.

en alētheia.

in truth. ἐν ἀφθαρσίᾳ.

en aphtharsia.

in incorruption.

The two sentences have a common structure. They begin with a reference to an abstract quality that God shows to human beings (mercy/grace), continue with a reference to the demonstration of that quality to “those who love” the Lord (him/our Lord Jesus Christ), and qualify the reference to love with an adverbial prepositional phrase of two words, “in” (ἐν) and an abstract noun (truth/incorruption) without the article.[7]

It is likely that this sort of expression was a known liturgical phrase among pious Jews in the first century BC since approximations of it appear elsewhere in the Psalms of Solomon:

4.25 Γένοιτο, κύριε, τὸ ἔλεός σου ἐπὶ

Genoito, kyrie, to eleos sou epi

πάντας τοὺς ἀγαπῶντάς σε.

pantas tous agapōntas se. O Lord, let your mercy come upon all those who love you.

10.3 Καὶ τὸ ἔλεος κυρίου ἐπὶ τοὺς

Kai to eleos kyriou epi tous

ἀγαπῶντας αὐτὸν ἐν ἀληθείᾳ.

agapōntas auton en alētheia. And the mercy of the Lord is upon those who love him in truth.

14.1 Πιστὸς κύριος τοῖς ἀγαπῶσιν αὐτὸν

Pistos kyrios tois agapōsin auton

ἐν ἀληθείᾳ, τοῖς ὑπομένουσιν

en alētheia, tois hypomenousin

παιδείαν αὐτοῦ.

paideian autou. Faithful is the Lord to those who love him in truth, to those who patiently endure his discipline

Paul probably knew similar expressions and formulated his concluding grace-wish with the same basic structure.[8] If so, then the prepositional phrase “in incorruption” should be attached to the expression “those who love,” and the term “incorruption” should probably be understood as a virtue, like truth, rather than as an eternal, incorruptible state. Like the Psalms of Solomon, Paul is describing the way in which those for whom he prays love God. Rather than saying that they love God “in truth” or “truly” (Pss. Sol. 6.6; 10.3; 14.1; OTP 2:658, 661, 663), he says that they love God “in incorruption,” that is, “in integrity” or “sincerely.”

Can the term ἀφθαρσία have this meaning? Earlier interpreters certainly thought so. Origen (Cels. 3.60) continued to see a reference to immortality in the use of the word here, but nevertheless he believed that it referred to being morally incorrupt (Heine 2002: 271–72). Ignatius seems to have used the term (although with no reference to Ephesians) to mean incorruption in the moral and doctrinal sense (Eph. 16.1–17.1; Magn. 6.2; Lightfoot 1890: 73; Moule 1953: 197). In the NT, the adjective ἄφθαρτος (aphthartos, incorruptible) seems to have both a moral and a temporal connotation in 1 Pet. 1:4, where it is associated with the terms ἀμίαντος (amiantos, undefiled) and ἀμάραντος (amarantos, unfading), and again in 1 Pet. 3:4, where it is associated with a gentle and quiet spirit. Since a moral meaning would parallel the reference to loving God “in truth” (that is, “truly” or “sincerely”) in the Psalms of Solomon, Paul probably intended the term to carry moral connotations here too.

Paul prays, then, for God to be gracious to those whose love for the Lord Jesus Christ is “free from every element liable to corruption” (Westcott 1906: 100).[9] He is certainly not tacking on to the grace of God—in contradiction to 2:1–10—an eleventh-hour condition of perfect love for the Lord. He is instead closing his letter with an implicit admonition to love the Lord Jesus Christ simply and purely, in a way untainted by the futility, darkness, and alienation that characterized his readers’ lives (2:1–3; 4:17–19; 5:8–12, 16; cf. 6:12) before they experienced the grace, love, and peace of God through their faith in the gospel.

Summary

Paul concludes the letter with a succinct prayer that concisely expresses three concerns. First, he asks that all believers might experience peace, which, in the context of the preceding letter, refers to peace with one another and peace with God. Second, he is concerned that the faith all believers have might bring love into their lives, which, again, in the context of the letter, refers to practical expressions of love for one another and to the personal experience of God’s love. Third, Paul prays that all those who have a sincere love for Jesus Christ might experience the grace of God. He prays, in other words, that all believers might know God’s immeasurable benevolence to his people both in giving them salvation and in equipping them to fulfill the role that God intends for his human creation and for his people, the church.



Additional Note

6:24. The letter ends with ἀμήν in some witnesses from the Alexandrian (Ψ, 1739), Western (D), and Byzantine traditions (most). Correctors of א and 1739 also inserted the term. The early date and geographical spread of the manuscripts that omit the term, however, push the evidence heavily in favor of its omission. These include the Alexandrian manuscripts 𝔓46, א, A, B, 33, 81, 1175, and 1739 and the Western manuscripts F and G. Among the Pauline Letters, only Galatians and Romans seem to have ended with ἀμήν (Best 1998: 620), and it is easy to imagine the term creeping into the copies of other letters as a result of the liturgical reading of the text (Metzger 1994: 543).
